paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-43 (MRT43) is characterized by intellectual disability or learning difficulties. It was first described as nonsyndromic (Ropers et al., 2011). Later reports described motor problems, including clumsiness, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria (Courtland et al., 2021). Some patients have a syndromic presentation with dysmorphic features, macrocephaly or microcephaly, skeletal anomalies, subependymal heterotopic nodules, or skeletal muscle involvement (Assoum et al., 2020; Gangfuss et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Assoum et al. (2020) reported 3 patients with syndromic intellectual disability. Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules. The younger sister also had congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. The third patient was 34 years old and had mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly. Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that the disorder has a heterogeneous phenotype and that more case descriptions are needed to refine it.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively reviewed clinical findings from 7 Omani children who were homozygous for the WASHC4 c.3056C-G mutation. Developmental delay or learning difficulties had been the main reason for medical evaluation, but all of the patients also had motor symptoms (mean age, 10.4 years). Their movements were described as clumsy, and clinical examination showed notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. The patients were then an average of 21 years old, and recent communication with their parents revealed no notable worsening of symptoms.

paragraphs.text: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing. After filtering for SNPs, only 2 changes remained. One was a homozygous nonsynonymous change in the SWIP (WASHC4) gene, which the authors considered causative based on high pathogenicity and conservation scores and functional considerations. The mutation led to significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and endosomal transport. Courtland et al. (2021) later identified this mutation as c.3056C-G (P1019R) and noted that cell lines from the patients showed decreased abundance of WASH proteins.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) proposed that SWIP P1019R causes loss of WASH complex function. In their model, this loss disrupts the endo-lysosomal pathway and leads to gradual accumulation of neurodegenerative markers, including unfolded protein response modulators, lysosomal enzymes, lipofuscin, and cleaved caspase-3, which results in cognitive deficits and progressive motor impairment. The human mutation has not been classified as a neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL). However, the authors noted that features of their mutant mouse model, including lipofuscin accumulation, closely resembled the NCLs.

paragraphs.text: Gangfuss et al. (2022) performed proteomic profiling of fibroblasts from a WASHC4-deficient patient and found dysregulation of proteins important for maintaining the neuromuscular axis. Histologic studies and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopy supported a role for WASHC4 in protein processing and clearance in humans.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) used CRISPR to introduce a CCT-to-CGT point mutation into exon 29 of mouse Washc4, creating a model of the human c.3056C-G mutation. In whole-brain lysate from homozygous mutant mice, the WASH complex members Strumpellin and WASH1 were markedly reduced (3.8% and 1.1% of wildtype, respectively), matching findings in the human patients. Quantitative spatial proteomics showed that 23 of 49 protein covariation modules differed between mutant and wildtype brain. A WASH/endosomal module was significantly decreased, and a lysosomal module containing cathepsins, hydrolases, and progranulin was significantly increased.

They also had fewer but larger cathepsin D-positive lysosomal puncta (Courtland et al., 2021). At 10 months of age, but not in adolescence, mutant mice had significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining selectively in the motor cortex (44.01% vs 25.38% of nuclei). Electron microscopy of motor cortex from 7-month-old mutant mice showed larger and more numerous electron-dense lipofuscin deposits.

paragraphs.text: On behavioral testing, the mutant mice performed normally on novel object recognition and the Y-maze (Courtland et al., 2021). However, they had a persistent deficit in cued fear memory recall in both adolescence and adulthood, despite intact responses to footshock and tones. Motor function was impaired and worsened over time: rotarod retention was reduced by nearly 50% at both ages, and gait abnormalities (longer swing time, longer strides, and reduced homologous coupling) appeared in adulthood.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic intellectual disability, Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsynonymous change in the SWIP (WASHC4) gene. The mutation led to significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the WASH complex. Courtland et al. (2021) later identified this mutation as c.3056C-G (P1019R).

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) re-evaluated 7 Omani children who were homozygous for a c.3056C-G transversion in the WASHC4 gene, resulting in a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution. The children had developmental delay or learning difficulties and motor symptoms, including clumsiness, fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. In HEK cells, the mutant protein co-immunoprecipitated less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wildtype (54.8% and 41.4% of wildtype, respectively). Mice homozygous for the corresponding mutation had markedly reduced brain levels of Strumpellin and WASH1, endo-lysosomal abnormalities, a cued fear memory deficit, and progressive motor dysfunction.

checks.claim: Courtland et al. (2021) re-evaluated 7 Omani children homozygous for a c.3056C-G transversion in the WASHC4 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from seven children with homozygous WASHC4c.3056C>G mutations (obtained by Dr. Rajab in 2010 at the Royal Hospital, Muscat, Oman).
checks.explanation: A C>G change is a transversion, so the wording follows directly.

checks.claim: The WASHC4 c.3056C-G transversion results in a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: an autosomal recessive mutation in WASHC4 (c.3056C>G; p.Pro1019Arg) was identified in a cohort of children with non-syndromic intellectual disability
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The Omani children homozygous for WASHC4 P1019R had developmental delay or learning difficulties.
checks.evidence_quote: While developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary impetus for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: The Omani children homozygous for WASHC4 P1019R had motor symptoms including clumsiness, fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria.
checks.evidence_quote: The patients’ movements were described as ‘clumsy’ with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: In HEK cells, the WASHC4 P1019R mutant protein co-immunoprecipitated less Strumpellin than wildtype (54.8% of wildtype).
checks.evidence_quote: Compared to WT, MUT SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 (IP: 54.8% and 41.4% of WT SWIP, respectively)
checks.explanation: Stated directly, in HEK cells.

checks.claim: In HEK cells, the WASHC4 P1019R mutant protein co-immunoprecipitated less WASH1 than wildtype (41.4% of wildtype).
checks.evidence_quote: Compared to WT, MUT SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 (IP: 54.8% and 41.4% of WT SWIP, respectively)
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Mice homozygous for the mutation corresponding to WASHC4 P1019R had markedly reduced brain levels of Strumpellin and WASH1.
checks.evidence_quote: Strumpellin (WT 100.0±5.1%, MUT 3.8±0.9%, t2.14=18.60, p=0.0021) and WASH1 (WT 100.0±4.3%, MUT 1.1±0.4%, t2.1=22.77, p=0.0018) were significantly decreased.
checks.explanation: Western blot of brain lysate from adult homozygous mutant mice; the reduction is marked.

checks.claim: Mice homozygous for the mutation corresponding to WASHC4 P1019R had endo-lysosomal abnormalities.
checks.evidence_quote: Cellular and histological analyses confirm that SWIPP1019R results in endo-lysosomal disruption and uncover indicators of neurodegeneration.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Mice homozygous for the mutation corresponding to WASHC4 P1019R had a cued fear memory deficit.
checks.evidence_quote: However, in a fear conditioning task, MUT mice displayed a significant deficit in cued fear memory (Figure 7).
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Mice homozygous for the mutation corresponding to WASHC4 P1019R had progressive motor dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: We find that SWIPP1019R not only impacts cognition, but also causes significant progressive motor deficits in mice.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, with syndromic intellectual disability, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the WASHC4 gene: a gln442-to-ter (Q442X) nonsense mutation and an asp1048-to-gly (D1048G) missense mutation. Each mutation was inherited from one parent. Both sisters had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules.

checks.evidence_quote: Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, had a stop-gain and a missense variants, each inherited from one parent (p.(Gln442*) and p.(Asp1048Gly)).

paragraphs.text: In a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the WASHC4 gene: a lys1079-to-arg (K1079R) substitution and a his503-to-arg (H503R) substitution. One mutation was inherited from each parent.
